displayQuote: A thing of beauty is a joy forever

meta.title: Who really said "A thing of beauty is a joy forever"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — it’s genuine John Keats. The opening line of his poem “Endymion” (1818). Keats wrote it “a joy for ever” (two words).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A thing of beauty is a joy for ever'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Keats: the first line of Endymion (1818). His original spelling was two words — “a joy for ever.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is the celebrated first line of Keats’s long poem Endymion: A Poetic Romance, published in 1818 by Taylor and Hessey. The attribution is verified against the poem’s text — though Keats wrote it as two words, “a joy for ever.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Endymion: A Poetic Romance (Book I, line 1)

source.excerpt:
A thing of beauty is a joy for ever:
Its loveliness increases; it will never
Pass into nothingness; but still will keep
A bower quiet for us, and a sleep
Full of sweet dreams, and health, and quiet breathing.
trail: The line opens Book I of Endymion; the full first-edition text (Taylor and Hessey, 1818) is on Project Gutenberg, reading “A thing of beauty is a joy for ever.”
Wikipedia’s article on the poem confirms Keats’s authorship, the 1818 Taylor and Hessey publication, and quotes the opening line.
Phrase reference phrases.org.uk traces the saying to Keats’s Endymion (1818) and notes the original two-word “for ever.”
source.excerptNote: The opening five lines of Book I. Modern quotation almost always collapses “for ever” into “forever.”
source.rightsNote: Endymion was first published in 1818, so the poem and this line are firmly in the public domain worldwide.

author.name: John Keats
author.heading: About John Keats
author.bio: John Keats (1795–1821) was one of the leading English Romantic poets, alongside Byron and Shelley, though he died of tuberculosis in Rome at just 25. He drafted Endymion — a 4,000-line retelling of the Greek myth of the shepherd loved by the moon goddess — in 1817, opening it with this line as its keynote. His reputation, modest in his lifetime, grew enormously after his death, resting on odes such as “Ode on a Grecian Urn” and “To Autumn.”

misattribution.heading: Genuine — but usually mis-spelled and mis-framed
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Keats is correct. What gets altered is the wording and the context:

items.why: Keats wrote “a joy for ever” as two words; the near-universal modern form compresses it to “forever.” The 1818 first-edition text shows the two-word spelling.

The line is often treated as a free-standing aphorism about beautiful objects, when it is the philosophical keynote opening a 4,000-line mythological poem about beauty as lasting consolation, per the poem’s summary.

misattribution.truthLine: The bottom line: it really is Keats, the first line of Endymion (1818) — just remember he wrote “a joy for ever,” per the original text.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Keats began drafting Endymion in 1817 as a deliberate test of his own powers — “a trial of my Powers of Imagination,” he called it — and chose to open the whole work with a thesis statement: that beauty, unlike other pleasures, does not fade but accumulates, keeping “a bower quiet for us” against despair.

The poem was savaged by contemporary critics, but the opening line detached itself and became one of the most quoted sentences in English. It survives today as shorthand for the idea that something beautiful is a permanent gift — the argument Keats spends the next twenty-odd lines unfolding.
